name: Denjongke / Sikkimese Bhutia
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Yliniemi, Juha. 2021. A descriptive grammar of Denjongke (Sikkimese Bhutia). Himalayan Linguistics Archive 10. Santa Barbara: University of California. xxx+687 pp. doi:10.5070/H920146466 (CC-BY-NC-ND; identical §2.7 wording in the 2019 Helsinki PhD, pp. 64-65)
catalog_locator: §2.6.2 end (summary of tone and register) and §2.7 'Stress or tone', pp. 65-66
catalog_quote: In summary of tone and register, Denjongke words can be divided into high and low register. ... Pitch seems to be the decisive factor in disambiguation. Therefore, Denjongke may be called a tonal language. Pitch is only marginally contrastive within the same register. In disyllabic words, the difference between high and low tone is realized as a difference in pitch rise between the first syllable and the second syllable (low tone words have a lower starting point and a greater rise in pitch than high tone words). 2.7 Stress or tone. I have not found stress to be a useful category for describing Denjongke. ... There are, however, two reasons for not considering the pitch difference in disyllabic nouns in Denjongke as constituting stress. The first is that, Denjongke is sensitive to how much the pitch rises from the first syllable to the second one in disyllabic words (see §2.6.2), a distinction that is better described in terms of tone than stress. Second, the correlates of stress (pitch, intensity, vowel duration, vowel quality) are inconsistently pronounced in disyllabic words, especially when comparing words pronounced in context with those pronounced in isolation. Similarly to stress in Balti (Caplow 2016), tone in verbs occurs on the first syllable, i.e. the monosyllabic verb root, whereas the tonally neutral verbal suffix attached to the verb may receive various pitches, depending on the intonational contexts.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (722 PDF pages, text, no scanned needed) and extracted pp. 96-99 with extracted text. §2.7 'Stress or tone' begins at the foot of printed p. 65 (PDF 97) and continues on printed p. 66 (PDF 98). The quoted sentences are there verbatim: 'I have not found stress to be a useful category for describing Denjongke.'.. 'There are, however, two reasons for not considering the pitch difference in disyllabic nouns in Denjongke as constituting stress. The first is that, Denjongke is sensitive to how much the pitch rises from the first syllable to the second one in disyllabic words (see §2.6.2), a distinction that is better described in terms of tone than stress. Second, the correlates of stress…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Denjongke is a two-register (high/low) tone language (register largely predictable from the initial consonant, pitch decisive in some minimal pairs). The author explicitly declines to posit word stress: disyllabic nouns in clausal context show a low-high pitch pattern (higher pitch on the second syllable), but this is analysed as the tonal pitch-rise contrast, not stress, and the usual stress correlates are inconsistent between isolation and context. In verbs the tone sits on the monosyllabic root (first syllable); verbal suffixes are tonally neutral and take pitch from intonation. The 2005 MA thesis (§5.6, p. 59) says the same more bluntly: stress 'seems to be a non-significant category in Denjongka words'.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated as exceptions; the author notes that in isolation the first syllable of high-tone disyllabic nouns is sometimes at equal pitch with the second, and that the verb suffix -di/ti may be higher or lower in pitch than the root depending on intonation (§2.7, §16.7).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (disyllabic nouns and verb root + suffix), compared in isolation vs. carrier-sentence context; based on instrumental (Praat) study of 29 disyllabic nouns with one speaker plus other speakers (§2.6.2).
new_statements.identity_note: Denjongke / Sikkimese Bhutia / Lhoke = Sikkimese sikk1242 (ISO sip); Yliniemi describes the language of Sikkim generally (fieldwork with speakers from several parts of Sikkim), not a single named dialect. Sandberg's 'Sikkim-Bhutia / Dé-jong Ké' is the same language. The LSI 'Bhotia' sketches (Sikkim, West Bengal) cover the same language as spoken in Sikkim and the Darjeeling hills.

tone_statements.citation: Guillemot, Céleste; Lee, Seunghun J. 2024. Phonetic Variation of Voiceless Nasals in Drenjongke (Bhutia). アジア・アフリカ言語文化研究 別冊 / Journal of Asian and African Studies, Supplement 4: 107-127. Tokyo: Research Institute for Languages and Cultures of Asia and Africa (ILCAA), Tokyo University of Foreign Studies. doi:10.15026/0002000630
tone_statements.quote: Lastly, tone is contrastive in syllables with a vowel only or with a nasal onset; Drenjongke has a two-tone system, high and low. Syllables can also be high or low register. In the transcriptions in this paper, high tone is indicated by an acute accent, and low by a grave accent on the vowel. Tone patterns with laryngeal categories are post-lexical; a syllable with an onset that is a voiceless or an aspirated consonant is followed by a high tone, while when the onset is a voiced and voiced aspirate consonant it bears a low tone. [...] (p. 113) Voiced nasals can bear either a high or low tone (as exemplified in 2a). However, voiceless nasals, like other voiceless phonemes in Drenjongke, exclusively belong to the high register.
tone_statements.locator: Section 2 (language background), last paragraph of p. 112 running onto p. 113; and p. 113 paragraph introducing example (2)
tone_statements.summary: Two tones (high vs low), lexically contrastive only with sonorant (nasal) or zero onsets; elsewhere determined by onset laryngeal class; voiceless nasals always high register.

tone_statements.citation: Lee, Seunghun J; Villegas, Julián; Namgyal, Kunzang. 2023. Tonal Contrast in Drenjongke (Bhutia): an Electroglottographic Study. In: Proceedings of the Second International Conference on Tone and Intonation (TAI 2023), 19-23. ISCA. doi:10.21437/TAI.2023-5
tone_statements.quote: Drenjongke is a two-tone language with high (H) and low (L) tones, which have different statuses depending on the onset consonant of a syllable. Syllables with a sonorant onset, including onsetless syllables, show a lexical tonal contrast. Syllables with an obstruent onset display an interaction between consonants and tone: voiceless unaspirated and aspirated onsets are followed by an H tone, while voiced unaspirated and aspirated onsets have an L tone following the onset.
tone_statements.summary: Two level tones, high and low. The contrast is lexical in syllables with a sonorant or zero onset; after obstruents tone follows the onset (voiceless > high, voiced and voiced aspirate > low).

tone_statements.citation: Villegas, Julián; Lee, Seunghun J. 2019. An electroglottograph study of tonal contrast in Drenjongke (Bhutia). In: Proceedings of the Seoul International Conference on Speech Sciences 2019 (SICSS 2019), Seoul National University, 15-16 November 2019, p. 27. Seoul: Korean Society of Speech Sciences.
tone_statements.quote: Drenjongke (Bhutia) is a Tibeto-Burman language spoken in Sikkim, India. Drenjongke is described as a tonal language with a contrast between high (H) and low (L) tone. An impressionistic study [2] report that Htoned syllables are accompanied with a glottal gesture, while L-tone syllables have breathy phonation, in addition to the difference in F0. … The results from six Drenjongke speakers indicate that Drenjongke may utilize phonation types in addition to F0, as described in [2].
tone_statements.locator: p. 27 (one-page abstract, opening paragraph and conclusion)
tone_statements.summary: Two tones, high and low; high tone reported with a glottal gesture and low tone with breathy phonation besides F0; EGG data from six speakers show a small open-quotient difference. Nothing on stress.

tone_statements.citation: Lee, Seunghun J; Hwang, Hyun Kyung; Monou, Tomoko; Kawahara, Shigeto. 2018. The phonetic realization of tonal contrast in Dränjongke. In: Proceedings of the 6th International Symposium on Tonal Aspects of Languages (TAL 2018), Berlin, 18-20 June 2018, 217-221. ISCA. doi:10.21437/TAL.2018-44
tone_statements.quote: Dra¨njongke is a Tiberto-Burman language spoken in Sikkim, India. The language has been described as having a two-way tonal contrast [1], but how the tonal contrast is realized phonetically has not been explored in detail. [...] The results suggest that (i) in syllables consisting of only vowels (e.g. [a]), the tonal differences manifest themselves at the left edge of syllables, and more surprisingly, (ii) in syllables with sonorant onsets (e.g. [na]), the tonal differences primarily appear during the sonorant intervals, and can be neutralized during the vocalic intervals.
tone_statements.locator: abstract, ISCA Archive landing page (paper pp. 217-221)
tone_statements.summary: 2-way tonal contrast (H vs L register), phonetically anchored at the syllable's left edge / onset consonant; acoustic F0 study.

tone_statements.quote: For example, only H-tones are allowed after voiceless and aspirated consonants in Dzongkha and Dränjongke. [...] (p. 128) Both speakers in Dränjongke, as well as our Dzongkha speaker, show a very clear f0 separation between H-toned and L-toned syllables during the onset consonant intervals. Speaker 2 of Dränjongke neutralizes the difference during the vowel intervals.
tone_statements.locator: p. 127 (Background, para 1) and p. 128 (first paragraph under Figure 1)
tone_statements.summary: Two tones (H, L); tone restricted by onset laryngeal class (voiceless/aspirated -> H); tonal target realised from the left edge of the syllable, including on sonorant onsets.

tone_statements.citation: van Driem, George. 2016. The Phonology of Dränjoke. Unpublished manuscript. [cited as 'van Driem, George. 2016. The Phonology of Dränjoke. ms.' in Guillemot & Lee 2024: 127 and as 'van Driem 2016' in their text on vowel length]
tone_statements.quote: Drenjongke distinguishes two register tones, high and low. The Drenjongke initials /k, kh, c, ch, t, th, p, ph, tr, thr, ts, tsh, sh, s, hr, lh, hng, hny, hn, hm, h, ʔ/ are inherently followed by the high register tone. The Drenjongke initials /g’, g, j’, j, d’, d, b’, b, dr’, dr, dz, zh, z, zh’, z’, r/ are invariably followed by the low register tone. The Drenjongke continuant initial phonemes /y, w, l, ng, ny, n, m/ may occur in either high register or low register tone syllables.
tone_statements.locator: p. 9, section 'Drenjongke phonology', first paragraph; vowel-onset register p. 10-11 and p. 15
tone_statements.summary: Two register tones, high and low; register is fixed after obstruent initials and contrasts after continuant onsets /y w l ng ny n m/ and vowel onsets; minor syllables may take the preceding tone.

tone_statements.citation: Baskaran, S. Ganesh. 2011. Bhotia. In Linguistic Survey of India: West Bengal Part-I, 571-627. ORGI.
tone_statements.quote: The Bhotia has three tones, which are contrastive viz, level tone, Rising tone and Falling tone. Level tone is the same on the pitch level of the normal speech. In the rising tone, the pitch suddenly rises from the level. In the falling tone there is a sudden fall of the pitch from the level. In Bhotia every vowel possesses any one of the above mentioned three tones occurring in different position in the words. Falling tone doesnot occur in the initial position of the word.

sources.quote: Drenjongke distinguishes two register tones, high and low. The Drenjongke initials /k, kh, c, ch, t, th, p, ph, tr, thr, ts, tsh, sh, s, hr, lh, hng, hny, hn, hm, h, ʔ/ are inherently followed by the high register tone. The Drenjongke initials /g’, g, j’, j, d’, d, b’, b, dr’, dr, dz, zh, z, zh’, z’, r/ are invariably followed by the low register tone. The Drenjongke continuant initial phonemes /y, w, l, ng, ny, n, m/ may occur in either high register or low register tone syllables.
